C0.note: Voting rule (veto core) computation, selection and manipulation.

C1.quote: a polynomial-time algorithm for the veto core exists
C1.note: Main results: polynomial algorithm (AL), manipulation by pessimist (SB), IC simulations and asymptotic analysis (SI), properties such as anonymity/neutrality (AX, minor).

C2.4.note: The rule is applied directly to preferences; no statement on reporting versus holding apart from the manipulation section.

C3.1.quote: a pessimist can manipulate the veto core in polynomial time
C3.1.note: Only the manipulation section considers misreporting; computation and selection do not.

C3.2.loc: Preliminaries; Computing the Veto Core; Selecting; Conclusion
C3.2.note: No statement that voters submit their held preferences in non-strategic analyses.

C4.1.note: The paper uses no voter utility or welfare notion. 'Happiness of the minority' is mentioned only in future directions.

C5.1.note: Results concern the veto core and its blocking guarantees, not evaluation by welfare, satisfaction or distortion. Representation/fairness claims appear in the introduction.

VOT.quote_behav: an agent’s strategies are limited to either blocking a candidate
VOT.quote_info: Consider a profile P where c is the worst element
VOT.note: Voters are non-strategic in the computation sections; the manipulator is strategic and knows the whole profile (inferable from the model).

C8.1.quote: It can be determined whether the veto core is manipulable by a pessimist
C8.1.note: Manipulation is studied as an existence-of-action problem, in the Duggan-Schwartz framework.

C8.2.note: Manipulation by optimist/pessimist is named explicitly.

claims.quote: veto-based rules – giving individuals or groups the ability to strike off certain candidates
a natural and effective way of ensuring that no minority is left
settings where the happiness of the minority matters, e.g. in group recommender systems

C9.1.note: Claims about protecting minorities and about when to use the rule.

C9.2.quote: ensuring that no minority is left with an outcome they find untenable
C9.2.note: The claim that minorities avoid untenable outcomes requires that ballots reflect voters' true preferences (sincere reporting) and that bottom-ranked candidates are those found unacceptable. The paper states neither.

C10.1.note: No statement of a purely procedural reading.
